# static_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/static_assertions/^1.1/

## Expand description

Assertions to ensure correct assumptions about constants, types, and more.

*All* checks provided by this crate are performed at [compile-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compile_time). This
allows for finding errors quickly and early when it comes to ensuring
certain features or aspects of a codebase. These macros are especially
important when exposing a public API that requires types to be the same size
or implement certain traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This crate is available [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/static_assertions) and can be used by adding the
following to your project’s [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html):

```
[dependencies]
static_assertions = "1.1.0"
```
and this to your crate root (`main.rs` or `lib.rs`):

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate static_assertions;
```
When using [Rust 2018 edition](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2018/12/06/Rust-1.31-and-rust-2018.html#rust-2018), the following shorthand can help if
having `#[macro_use]` is undesirable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Very thorough examples are provided in the docs for
[each individual macro](https://docs.rs#macros). Failure case examples are also documented.

[§](https://docs.rs#changes)Changes

See [ CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/nvzqz/static-assertions-rs/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md)
for an exhaustive list of what has changed from one version to another.

[§](https://docs.rs#donate)Donate

This project is made freely available (as in free beer), but unfortunately
not all beer is free! So, if you would like to buy me a beer (or coffee or
*more*), then consider supporting my work that’s benefited your project
and thousands of others.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_cfg.html)- cfg
- Asserts that a given configuration is set.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_align.html)- eq_ - align
- Asserts that types are equal in alignment.

- Asserts that the type has the given fields.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_all.html)- impl_ - all
- Asserts that the type implements *all*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_any.html)- impl_ - any
- Asserts that the type implements *any*of the given traits.

# variadics_please - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/variadics_please/latest/target-redirect/variadics_please/

## Expand description

Provides macros for implementing traits on variadic types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples.html)- tuples
- Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids. Useful to generate scaffolding to work around Rust
lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`. If you require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples_with_size!`
- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples_enumerated.html)- tuples_ - enumerated
- A variant of `all_tuples!`
- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples_with_size.html)- tuples_ - with_ - size
- Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids with their length. Useful to generate scaffolding to
work around Rust lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples_with_size!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`preceded by their length. If you don’t require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples!`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# sidereon_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon-core)sidereon-core

The complete Sidereon engine in one crate. It folds the numerical astrodynamics core (orbit propagation, force models, frames, time, SGP4) together with the GNSS domain layer (SP3, broadcast ephemeris, multi-GNSS positioning, RTK/PPP, ionosphere/troposphere, DOP).

- The propagation/astro layer is always present under the `astro`
- The GNSS layer lives behind the default-on `gnss`cargo feature, so a propagation-only consumer can build with`--no-default-features`(plus any astro features it wants) and never compile the IONEX/SP3 parsers.

The GNSS façade is organized by user-facing tasks:

- `ephemeris`
- `rinex`
- `antex`
- `combinations`
- `observables`
- `velocity`
- `positioning`
- `dgnss`
- `quality`
- `observation_qc`
- `signal`
- `ppp_corrections`
- `atmosphere`
- `orbit`

Implementation modules (`sp3`, `rinex_nav`, `spp`, etc.) are crate-private.
This is a clean public surface rather than a compatibility shim around the
original implementation-shaped module layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#units-policy-internal-representation)Units policy (internal representation)

All quantities are stored and computed in **SI base units**, with the frame
and datum encoded in the type name (per the spec’s frames-in-the-type-system
rule), never hidden behind a bare `position_m`:

- **Length / position:**meters (- `_m`). SP3 positions are ITRF/IGS-frame ECEF meters; SPP receiver positions are WGS84/ITRF-compatible ECEF meters. (The- `astro`
- **Time / clock:**seconds (- `_s`). Epochs are represented by the- `astro`- `Instant`/- `TimeScale`), always scale-tagged; there is no bare ambiguous epoch.
- **Velocity:**meters per second (- `_m_s`).
- **Angles:**radians (- `_rad`) internally. Degrees appear only at I/O edges and are named- `_deg`.
- **Frequency:**hertz (- `_hz`).

Field and parameter names carry the unit suffix so the unit is visible at
every call site. Matrix/vector linear algebra uses `nalgebra`
(`DMatrix`/`DVector`) per the spec.

# everruns_integrations_browserless - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-browserless/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_browserless/

## Expand description

Browserless Integration

Cloud browser automation via Browserless REST API and CDP (WebSocket) sessions. Supports screenshots, DOM reading, structured scraping, and multi-step interactions (click, type, keyboard, mouse, touch).

Two modes:

- **REST**(default): Each tool call uses a fresh ephemeral browser. No state, no cleanup.
- **CDP sessions**:- `browserless_open_browser`opens a persistent browser via WebSocket. Subsequent tool calls reuse it (preserving login, cookies, navigation history).- `browserless_close_browser`releases the browser.

Decision: External integration crate, auto-registered via inventory plugin system Decision: REST for one-shot operations, CDP WebSocket for persistent browser sessions Decision: /function endpoint for multi-step interactions (click, type, navigate) Decision: CDP sessions use Browserless.reconnect to keep browser alive between tool calls

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cdp](https://docs.rs/cdp/index.html)
- Minimal Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) client over WebSocket.
- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- Browserless API client.
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- [session_](https://docs.rs/session_tools/index.html)- tools
- CDP session management tools: open_browser and close_browser.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Browserless API key resolution, browser session state, and parameter helpers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [browserless_](https://docs.rs/fn.browserless_api_base.html)- api_ - base
- REST API base URL. Reads `BROWSERLESS_API_BASE`env var with fallback to the default production SFO endpoint. Strips trailing slashes and falls back to the default if the env var is empty.
- [browserless_](https://docs.rs/fn.browserless_ws_base.html)- ws_ - base
- WebSocket base URL. Reads `BROWSERLESS_WS_BASE`env var with fallback to the default production SFO endpoint. Strips trailing slashes and falls back to the default if the env var is empty.

# sourceatlas 0.2.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sourceatlas/0.2.2

# SourceAtlas

SourceAtlas is a command-line tool written in Rust that scans a source code repository and generates useful statistics.

I started this project as a way to learn Rust by building something practical instead of only completing exercises. The goal isn't to compete with existing tools, but to build a clean, well-structured application while learning more about idiomatic Rust and software engineering.

## Features

Current features include:

- Recursive directory scanning
- Ignores common build and IDE directories:
- `target`
- `build`
- `node_modules`
- `.idea`
- `.vscode`

- Reports:
- Directories scanned
- Files scanned
- Files analyzed
- Files skipped
- Total lines

- Gracefully skips unreadable or binary files
- Unit tested

## Installation

Install from crates.io:

```
```
Or build from source:

```
```
## Usage

Scan the current directory:

```
```
Scan another directory:

```
```
## Example Output

```
-------------
|SourceAtlas|
-------------
Scanning Git repo
LANGUAGE STATS
Rust: 100.0%
DIRECTORIES
--------
total directories: 4
TOTALS
--------
total files found: 13
total files analyzed: 7
total files skipped: 6
total lines: 425
```
*The above output is generated when running SourceAtlas on itself*

## Roadmap

Some features I'd like to add:

- More visually appealing report generation
- Custom ignore files
- JSON output
- Markdown reports

# ferrocat-cli 2.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ferrocat-cli/2.1.0

# ferrocat-cli

Command-line interface for Ferrocat catalog workflows.

The first supported workflow is `ferrocat audit`, a CI-oriented release gate
for source and target catalogs:

```
```
`ferrocat-cli` releases include a prebuilt `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` archive
named `ferrocat-<version>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz`. The release
workflow smoke-tests the packaged `ferrocat` binary before uploading it.

Exit codes:

- `0`: audit completed with no error diagnostics
- `1`: audit completed and reported at least one error diagnostic
- `2`: command usage, I/O, parse, or serialization failure

Use `--format json` when CI should consume the structured
`CatalogAuditReport`.

# everruns_integrations_parallel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-parallel/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_parallel/

## Expand description

Parallel web search and fetch for Everruns agents.

`everruns-integrations-parallel` is part of the
[Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem. It contributes
[Parallel](https://parallel.ai)’s hosted MCP server so agents get
provider-owned `web_search` and `web_fetch` tools — free by default, with an
optional Parallel API-key connection for authenticated usage.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_core::capabilities::Capability;
use everruns_integrations_parallel::ParallelCapability;
let capability = ParallelCapability;
assert_eq!(capability.id(), "parallel_search");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-notes)Design notes

- Uses Parallel’s hosted MCP server directly, so Everruns gets the provider-owned behavior without proxying or reimplementing it.
- Defaults to the free unauthenticated endpoint. Per-capability config can require a user-scoped Parallel API-key connection and switch to the OAuth-compatible MCP endpoint.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use payments::`- [ParallelPaymentsCapability](https://docs.rs/payments/struct.ParallelPaymentsCapability.html);

# azalea_reflection_proxy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/azalea-reflection-proxy/0.1.2/azalea_reflection_proxy/

## Expand description

azalea-reflection-proxy — spectate and control an azalea bot session through a local reflection proxy. Rust port of aesthetic0001/mineflayer-reflection-proxy.

The proxy owns the single real (Microsoft-authed) connection to the
target server. Your bot connects to the proxy locally as an offline
client and becomes the controller; vanilla clients that join the
same local address become spectators, see the bot as a live player
entity, and can take over with `,acquire`.

```
use azalea_reflection_proxy::ReflectionProxy;
let proxy = ReflectionProxy::builder()
    .target("mc.hypixel.net")
    .email("you@example.com")
    .spawn()
    .await?;
// then point your azalea bot at it instead of the real server:
//   ClientBuilder::new()
//       .set_handler(handle)
//       .start(Account::offline("reflected"), proxy.local_addr())
// and add a vanilla-client server entry for the same address to
// spectate. proxy.local_addr() is a real SocketAddr, so a bound
// port of 0 picks a free one.
```

# mirui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mirui/0.39.0/mirui/

## Expand description

mirui — a `no_std`, ECS-driven UI framework for embedded, desktop,
and (planned) WebAssembly. Renders with 24.8 fixed-point subpixel
precision on a software rasterizer designed for MCUs without an FPU;
optionally runs on top of SDL2 (CPU or hardware-accelerated) on
desktop.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
[dependencies]
mirui = { version = "0.39", features = ["sdl"] }
```
The snippet below builds against mirui’s default features and is
verified by `cargo test --doc`. Swap `FramebufSurface` for
`mirui::surface::sdl::SdlSurface::new("hello", 480, 320)` (with the
`sdl` feature) to run on a desktop window instead of into a
user-supplied flush callback.

```
use mirui::prelude::*;
use mirui::surface::framebuf::FramebufSurface;
use mirui::render::texture::ColorFormat;
use mirui::types::Rect;
let backend = FramebufSurface::with_format(
    480, 320, ColorFormat::RGBA8888,
    |_bytes: &[u8], _area: &Rect| { /* push to your display */ },
);
let mut app = App::new(backend);
app.with_default_widgets().with_default_systems();
let root = app.spawn_root().id();
ui! {
    :(
        parent: root
        world: &mut app.world
    :)
    header (
        bg_color: ColorToken::Primary,
        text_color: ColorToken::OnPrimary,
        text: "Hello mirui!",
        border_radius: 8
    ) {}
};
app.run();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#other-targets)Other targets

mirui also runs bare-metal on RISC-V and ARM Cortex-M MCUs through
[ surface::framebuf::FramebufSurface](https://docs.rs/surface/framebuf/struct.FramebufSurface.html), and a Cargo workspace
template builds the same UI code on both desktop and embedded
targets unchanged. The full walkthrough — including ESP32-C3
wiring, the workspace layout, and a recipe for adding new target
crates — lives in

[.](https://github.com/W-Mai/mirui/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)

`docs/quickstart.md`[§](https://docs.rs#module-map)Module map

- `render`- `render::backends`
- `input`- `input::feedback`

Provides macros for implementing traits on variadic types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples.html)- tuples
- Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids. Useful to generate scaffolding to work around Rust
lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`. If you require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples_with_size!`
- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples_enumerated.html)- tuples_ - enumerated
- A variant of `all_tuples!`
- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples_with_size.html)- tuples_ - with_ - size
- Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids with their length. Useful to generate scaffolding to
work around Rust lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples_with_size!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`preceded by their length. If you don’t require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples!`

[48](https://docs.rs#48)/// Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids. Useful to generate scaffolding to work around Rust
[49](https://docs.rs#49)/// lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`
[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// invokes `impl_foo` providing ident tuples through arity `start..end`.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)/// If you require the length of the tuple, see [`all_tuples_with_size!`].
[52](https://docs.rs#52)///
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// # Examples
[54](https://docs.rs#54)///
[55](https://docs.rs#55)/// ## Single parameter
[56](https://docs.rs#56)///
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// ```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// # use core::marker::PhantomData;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// #
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// struct Foo<T> {
[62](https://docs.rs#62)///     // ..
[63](https://docs.rs#63)/// #    _phantom: PhantomData<T>
[64](https://docs.rs#64)/// }
[65](https://docs.rs#65)///
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// trait WrappedInFoo {
[67](https://docs.rs#67)///     type Tup;
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)///
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// macro_rules! impl_wrapped_in_foo {
[71](https://docs.rs#71)///     ($($T:ident),*) => {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///         impl<$($T),*> WrappedInFoo for ($($T,)*) {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///             type Tup = ($(Foo<$T>,)*);
[74](https://docs.rs#74)///         }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///     };
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// // start from 0 element to 15 elements
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// all_tuples!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 0, 15, T);
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!();
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0);
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0, T1);
[83](https://docs.rs#83)/// // ..
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0 .. T14);
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// ```
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// # Multiple parameters
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// ```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples;
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// #
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// trait Append {
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///     type Out<Item>;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)///     fn append<Item>(tup: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item>;
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)///
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// impl Append for () {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)///     type Out<Item> = (Item,);
[99](https://docs.rs#99)///     fn append<Item>(_: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///         (item,)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///     }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// }
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// macro_rules! impl_append {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)///     ($(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///         impl<$($P),*> Append for ($($P,)*) {
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///             type Out<Item> = ($($P),*, Item);
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///             fn append<Item>(($($p,)*): Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///                 ($($p),*, item)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)///             }
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///         }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///     }
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// }
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// // start from 1 element to 15 elements
[116](https://docs.rs#116)/// all_tuples!(impl_append, 1, 15, P, p);
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0));
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0), (P1, p1));
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0), (P1, p1), (P2, p2));
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// // ..
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P14, p14));
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// // start from 16 elements to 20
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// all_tuples!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P15, p15));
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// // ..
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// // impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P19, p19));
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// **`#[doc(fake_variadic)]`**
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// To improve the readability of your docs when implementing a trait for
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// tuples or fn pointers of varying length you can use the rustdoc-internal `fake_variadic` marker.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// All your impls are collapsed and shown as a single `impl Trait for (F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ)`.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///
[136](https://docs.rs#136)/// The `all_tuples!` macro does most of the work for you, the only change to your implementation macro
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// is that you have to accept attributes using `$(#[$meta:meta])*`.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// Since this feature requires a nightly compiler, it's only enabled on docs.rs by default.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// Add the following to your lib.rs if not already present:
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// ```
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// // `rustdoc_internals` is needed for `#[doc(fake_variadics)]`
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// #![cfg_attr(any(docsrs, docsrs_dep), feature(rustdoc_internals))]
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// ```
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// ```
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// #
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// trait Variadic {}
[151](https://docs.rs#151)///
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// impl Variadic for () {}
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// macro_rules! impl_variadic {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)///     ($(#[$meta:meta])* $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)///         $(#[$meta])*
[157](https://docs.rs#157)///         impl<$($P),*> Variadic for ($($P,)*) {}
[158](https://docs.rs#158)///     }
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)///
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// all_tuples!(#[doc(fake_variadic)] impl_variadic, 1, 15, P, p);
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// ```
[163](https://docs.rs#163)#[proc_macro]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)pub fn all_tuples(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    let input = match parse_all_tuples(input) {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        Ok(input) => input,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        Err(err) => {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            return err;
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    };
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    let ident_tuples = build_ident_tuples(&input);
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    let macro_ident = &input.macro_ident;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    let invocations = make_invocation_range(&input).map(|n| {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        let ident_tuples = choose_ident_tuples(&input, &ident_tuples, n);
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        let attrs = attrs(&input, n);
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        quote! { #macro_ident!(#attrs #ident_tuples); }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    });
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    TokenStream::from(quote! { #(#invocations)* })
[179](https://docs.rs#179)}
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// A variant of [`all_tuples!`] that enumerates its output.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// In particular, the tuples used by the inner macro will themselves be composed
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// of tuples which contain the index.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)///
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// For example, with a single parameter:
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// ```
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples_enumerated;
[189](https://docs.rs#189)///
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// trait Squawk {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)///     fn squawk(&self);
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// }
[193](https://docs.rs#193)///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// // If every type in a tuple is `Squawk`, the tuple can squawk by having its
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// // constituents squawk sequentially:
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// macro_rules! impl_squawk {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///     ($(($n:tt, $T:ident)),*) => {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)///         impl<$($T: Squawk),*> Squawk for ($($T,)*) {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)///             fn squawk(&self) {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)///                 $(
[201](https://docs.rs#201)///                     self.$n.squawk();
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///                 )*
[203](https://docs.rs#203)///             }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///         }
[205](https://docs.rs#205)///     };
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// }
[207](https://docs.rs#207)///
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 1, 15, T);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// // impl_squawk!((0, T0));
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// // impl_squawk!((0, T0), (1, T1));
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// // ..
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// // impl_squawk!((0, T0) .. (14, T14));
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 16, 20, T);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// // impl_append!((0, T0) .. (15, T15));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// // ..
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// // impl_append!((0, T0) .. (19, T19));
[218](https://docs.rs#218)/// ```
[219](https://docs.rs#219)///
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// With multiple parameters, the result is similar, but with the additional parameters
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// included in each tuple; e.g.:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// ```ignore
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 1, 15, P, p);
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// // impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0));
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// // impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0), (1, P1, p1));
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// // ..
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// // impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0) .. (14, P14, p14));
[228](https://docs.rs#228)///
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
[230](https://docs.rs#230)/// // impl_append!((0, P0, p0) .. (15, P15, p15));
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// // ..
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// // impl_append!((0, P0, p0) .. (19, P19, p19));
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// ```
[234](https://docs.rs#234)#[proc_macro]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)pub fn all_tuples_enumerated(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    let input = match parse_all_tuples(input) {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        Ok(input) => input,
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        Err(err) => {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            return err;
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    };
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    let ident_tuples = build_ident_tuples_enumerated(&input);
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    let macro_ident = &input.macro_ident;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    let invocations = make_invocation_range(&input).map(|n| {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        let ident_tuples = choose_ident_tuples_enumerated(&input, &ident_tuples, n);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        let attrs = attrs(&input, n);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        quote! { #macro_ident!(#attrs #ident_tuples); }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    });
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    TokenStream::from(quote! { #(#invocations)* })
[250](https://docs.rs#250)}
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids with their length. Useful to generate scaffolding to
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// work around Rust lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples_with_size!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// invokes `impl_foo` providing ident tuples through arity `start..end` preceded by their length.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)/// If you don't require the length of the tuple, see [`all_tuples!`].
[256](https://docs.rs#256)///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// # Examples
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// ## Single parameter
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)/// # use core::marker::PhantomData;
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples_with_size;
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// #
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// struct Foo<T> {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)///     // ..
[267](https://docs.rs#267)/// #    _phantom: PhantomData<T>
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)///
[270](https://docs.rs#270)/// trait WrappedInFoo {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)///     type Tup;
[272](https://docs.rs#272)///     const LENGTH: usize;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)///
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// macro_rules! impl_wrapped_in_foo {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)///     ($N:expr, $($T:ident),*) => {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)///         impl<$($T),*> WrappedInFoo for ($($T,)*) {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)///             type Tup = ($(Foo<$T>,)*);
[279](https://docs.rs#279)///             const LENGTH: usize = $N;
[280](https://docs.rs#280)///         }
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///     };
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)///
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// all_tuples_with_size!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 0, 15, T);
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(0);
[286](https://docs.rs#286)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(1, T0);
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(2, T0, T1);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)/// // ..
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(15, T0 .. T14);
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///
[291](https://docs.rs#291)/// all_tuples_with_size!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 16, 20, T);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(16, T0 .. T15);
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// // ..
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// // impl_wrapped_in_foo!(20, T0 .. T19);
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// ```
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// ## Multiple parameters
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// ```
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples_with_size;
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// #
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// trait Append {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///     type Out<Item>;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)///     fn append<Item>(tup: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item>;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// }
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// impl Append for () {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)///     type Out<Item> = (Item,);
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///     fn append<Item>(_: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///         (item,)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)///     }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// }
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// macro_rules! impl_append {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///     ($N:expr, $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)///         impl<$($P),*> Append for ($($P,)*) {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///             type Out<Item> = ($($P),*, Item);
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///             fn append<Item>(($($p,)*): Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///                 ($($p),*, item)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///             }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///         }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)///     }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// all_tuples_with_size!(impl_append, 1, 15, P, p);
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// // impl_append!(1, (P0, p0));
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// // impl_append!(2, (P0, p0), (P1, p1));
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// // impl_append!(3, (P0, p0), (P1, p1), (P2, p2));
[329](https://docs.rs#329)/// // ..
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// // impl_append!(15, (P0, p0) .. (P14, p14));
[331](https://docs.rs#331)///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// all_tuples_with_size!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
[333](https://docs.rs#333)/// // impl_append!(16, (P0, p0) .. (P15, p15));
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// // ..
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// // impl_append!(20, (P0, p0) .. (P19, p19));
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// ```
[337](https://docs.rs#337)///
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// **`#[doc(fake_variadic)]`**
[339](https://docs.rs#339)///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// To improve the readability of your docs when implementing a trait for
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// tuples or fn pointers of varying length you can use the rustdoc-internal `fake_variadic` marker.
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// All your impls are collapsed and shown as a single `impl Trait for (F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ)`.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// The `all_tuples!` macro does most of the work for you, the only change to your implementation macro
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// is that you have to accept attributes using `$(#[$meta:meta])*`.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// Since this feature requires a nightly compiler, it's only enabled on docs.rs by default.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// Add the following to your lib.rs if not already present:
[349](https://docs.rs#349)///
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// ```
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// // `rustdoc_internals` is needed for `#[doc(fake_variadics)]`
[352](https://docs.rs#352)/// #![cfg_attr(any(docsrs, docsrs_dep), feature(rustdoc_internals))]
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// ```
[354](https://docs.rs#354)///
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// # use variadics_please::all_tuples_with_size;
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// #
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// trait Variadic {}
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// impl Variadic for () {}
[361](https://docs.rs#361)///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// macro_rules! impl_variadic {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)///     ($N:expr, $(#[$meta:meta])* $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)///         $(#[$meta])*
[365](https://docs.rs#365)///         impl<$($P),*> Variadic for ($($P,)*) {}
[366](https://docs.rs#366)///     }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)/// }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)/// all_tuples_with_size!(#[doc(fake_variadic)] impl_variadic, 1, 15, P, p);
[370](https://docs.rs#370)/// ```
[371](https://docs.rs#371)#[proc_macro]
[372](https://docs.rs#372)pub fn all_tuples_with_size(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    let input = match parse_all_tuples(input) {
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        Ok(input) => input,
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        Err(err) => {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)            return err;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        }
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    };
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    let ident_tuples = build_ident_tuples(&input);
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    let macro_ident = &input.macro_ident;
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    let invocations = make_invocation_range(&input).map(|n| {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        let ident_tuples = choose_ident_tuples(&input, &ident_tuples, n);
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        let attrs = attrs(&input, n);
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        quote! { #macro_ident!(#n, #attrs #ident_tuples); }
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    });
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    TokenStream::from(quote! { #(#invocations)* })
[387](https://docs.rs#387)}
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)fn parse_all_tuples(input: TokenStream) -> std::result::Result<AllTuples, TokenStream> {
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    let ts: TokenStream2 = input.into();
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    let mut iter = ts.to_token_iter();
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    let tuples = AllTuplesParsed::parse(&mut iter).map_err(pretty_print_error)?;
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    let start: usize = match tuples.start.value().try_into() {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        Ok(start) => start,
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        Err(_) => {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)            return Err(span_error(
[397](https://docs.rs#397)                tuples.start,
[398](https://docs.rs#398)                "`start` should be in the range of 0..usize::MAX",
[399](https://docs.rs#399)            ));
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    };
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    let end: usize = match tuples.end.value().try_into() {
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        Ok(end) => end,
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        Err(_) => {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)            return Err(span_error(
[406](https://docs.rs#406)                tuples.end,
[407](https://docs.rs#407)                "`end` should be in the range of 0..usize::MAX",
[408](https://docs.rs#408)            ));
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        }
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    };
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    if end < start {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        return Err(span_error(tuples.end, "`start` should <= `end`"));
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    Ok(AllTuples {
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        fake_variadic: tuples.fake_variadic.is_some(),
[416](https://docs.rs#416)        macro_ident: tuples.macro_ident,
[417](https://docs.rs#417)        start,
[418](https://docs.rs#418)        end,
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        idents: tuples.idents.iter().map(|i| i.value.clone()).collect(),
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    })
[421](https://docs.rs#421)}
[422](https://docs.rs#422)
[423](https://docs.rs#423)/// Unfortunately there's no upstream pretty-printing in `unsynn` yet:
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// <https://seed.pipapo.org/nodes/seed.pipapo.org/rad:z39WbeupErKS8TwbDS5yU8eZSa3C/issues/960feccb89aef6452b5ec0a6ce6a00604c8d8d21>
[425](https://docs.rs#425)fn pretty_print_error(err: Error) -> TokenStream {
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    let span = err
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        .failed_at()
[428](https://docs.rs#428)        .map(|tt| tt.span())
[429](https://docs.rs#429)        .unwrap_or_else(Span::call_site);
[430](https://docs.rs#430)
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    let msg = match err.kind {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        ErrorKind::Other { reason } => reason,
[433](https://docs.rs#433)        ErrorKind::UnexpectedToken => format!("expected {}", err.expected_type_name()),
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        _ => err.to_string(),
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    };
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    quote::quote_spanned! { span => compile_error!(#msg); }.into()
[437](https://docs.rs#437)}
[438](https://docs.rs#438)
[439](https://docs.rs#439)fn span_error(tokens: impl ToTokens, msg: &str) -> TokenStream {
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    let span = tokens
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        .to_token_iter()
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        .next()
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        .map(|tt| tt.span())
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        .unwrap_or_else(Span::call_site);
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    quote::quote_spanned! { span => compile_error!(#msg); }.into()
[446](https://docs.rs#446)}
[447](https://docs.rs#447)
[448](https://docs.rs#448)fn build_ident_tuples(input: &AllTuples) -> Vec<TokenStream2> {
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    (0..input.end)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        .map(|i| {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            let idents = input
[452](https://docs.rs#452)                .idents
[453](https://docs.rs#453)                .iter()
[454](https://docs.rs#454)                .map(|ident| format_ident!("{}{}", ident, i));
[455](https://docs.rs#455)            to_ident_tuple(idents, input.idents.len())
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        })
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        .collect()
[458](https://docs.rs#458)}
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)fn build_ident_tuples_enumerated(input: &AllTuples) -> Vec<TokenStream2> {
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    (0..input.end)
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        .map(|i| {
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            let idents = input
[464](https://docs.rs#464)                .idents
[465](https://docs.rs#465)                .iter()
[466](https://docs.rs#466)                .map(|ident| format_ident!("{}{}", ident, i));

[469](https://docs.rs#469)        .collect()

[471](https://docs.rs#471)
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// Returns an iterator over the invocation arities, including the optional fake-variadic `n=1`.
[473](https://docs.rs#473)fn make_invocation_range(input: &AllTuples) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> {
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    let base = input.start..=input.end;
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    let extra: Vec<usize> = if input.fake_variadic && input.start > 1 {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        vec![1]
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    } else {
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        vec![]
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    };
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    base.chain(extra)
[481](https://docs.rs#481)}
[482](https://docs.rs#482)
[483](https://docs.rs#483)fn choose_ident_tuples(input: &AllTuples, ident_tuples: &[TokenStream2], n: usize) -> TokenStream2 {
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    // `rustdoc` uses the first ident to generate nice
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    // idents with subscript numbers e.g. (F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ).
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    // We don't want two numbers, so we use the
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    // original, unnumbered idents for this case.
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    if input.fake_variadic && n == 1 {
[489](https://docs.rs#489)        let ident_tuple = to_ident_tuple(input.idents.iter().cloned(), input.idents.len());
[490](https://docs.rs#490)        quote! { #ident_tuple }
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    } else {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        let ident_tuples = &ident_tuples[..n];
[493](https://docs.rs#493)        quote! { #(#ident_tuples),* }
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    }
[495](https://docs.rs#495)}
[496](https://docs.rs#496)
[497](https://docs.rs#497)fn choose_ident_tuples_enumerated(
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    input: &AllTuples,
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    ident_tuples: &[TokenStream2],
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    n: usize,
[501](https://docs.rs#501)) -> TokenStream2 {
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    if input.fake_variadic && n == 1 {
[503](https://docs.rs#503)        let ident_tuple = to_ident_tuple_enumerated(input.idents.iter().cloned(), 0);
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        quote! { #ident_tuple }
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    } else {
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        let ident_tuples = &ident_tuples[..n];
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        quote! { #(#ident_tuples),* }
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    }
[509](https://docs.rs#509)}
[510](https://docs.rs#510)
[511](https://docs.rs#511)fn to_ident_tuple(idents: impl Iterator<Item = Ident>, generic_num: usize) -> TokenStream2 {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    if generic_num < 2 {
[513](https://docs.rs#513)        quote! { #(#idents)* }
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    } else {
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        quote! { (#(#idents),*) }
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    }
[517](https://docs.rs#517)}
[518](https://docs.rs#518)
[519](https://docs.rs#519)/// Like `to_ident_tuple`, but it enumerates the identifiers
[520](https://docs.rs#520)fn to_ident_tuple_enumerated(idents: impl Iterator<Item = Ident>, idx: usize) -> TokenStream2 {
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    let idx = Literal::usize_unsuffixed(idx);
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    quote! { (#idx, #(#idents),*) }
[523](https://docs.rs#523)}
[524](https://docs.rs#524)
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// n: number of elements
[526](https://docs.rs#526)fn attrs(input: &AllTuples, n: usize) -> TokenStream2 {
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    if !input.fake_variadic {
[528](https://docs.rs#528)        return TokenStream2::default();
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    match n {
[531](https://docs.rs#531)        // An empty tuple (i.e. the unit type) is still documented separately,
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        // so no `#[doc(hidden)]` here.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)        0 => TokenStream2::default(),
[534](https://docs.rs#534)        n => {
[535](https://docs.rs#535)            let cfg = quote! { any(docsrs, docsrs_dep) };
[536](https://docs.rs#536)            // The `#[doc(fake_variadic)]` attr has to be on the first impl block.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)            if n == 1 {
[538](https://docs.rs#538)                let doc = Literal::string(&format!(
[539](https://docs.rs#539)                    "This trait is implemented for tuple{s1} {range} item{s2} long.",
[540](https://docs.rs#540)                    range = if input.start == input.end {
[541](https://docs.rs#541)                        format!("exactly {}", input.start)
[542](https://docs.rs#542)                    } else {
[543](https://docs.rs#543)                        format!(
[544](https://docs.rs#544)                            "{down}up to {up}",
[545](https://docs.rs#545)                            down = if input.start != 0 {
[546](https://docs.rs#546)                                format!("down to {} ", input.start)
[547](https://docs.rs#547)                            } else {
[548](https://docs.rs#548)                                "".to_string()
[549](https://docs.rs#549)                            },
[550](https://docs.rs#550)                            up = input.end
[551](https://docs.rs#551)                        )
[552](https://docs.rs#552)                    },
[553](https://docs.rs#553)                    s1 = if input.end > input.start { "s" } else { "" },
[554](https://docs.rs#554)                    s2 = if input.end >= input.start && input.end > 1 {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)                        "s"
[556](https://docs.rs#556)                    } else {
[557](https://docs.rs#557)                        ""
[558](https://docs.rs#558)                    }
[559](https://docs.rs#559)                ));
[560](https://docs.rs#560)                if input.start <= 1 && input.end >= 1 {
[561](https://docs.rs#561)                    // n == 1 and it's included
[562](https://docs.rs#562)                    quote! {
[563](https://docs.rs#563)                        #[cfg_attr(#cfg, doc(fake_variadic))]
[564](https://docs.rs#564)                        #[cfg_attr(#cfg, doc = #doc)]
[565](https://docs.rs#565)                    }
[566](https://docs.rs#566)                } else {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)                    // n == 1 but it's not included,
[568](https://docs.rs#568)                    // only generate if #cfg
[569](https://docs.rs#569)                    quote! {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)                        #[cfg(#cfg)]
[571](https://docs.rs#571)                        #[doc(fake_variadic)]
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                        #[doc = #doc]
[573](https://docs.rs#573)                    }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)                }
[575](https://docs.rs#575)            } else {
[576](https://docs.rs#576)                quote! { #[cfg_attr(#cfg, doc(hidden))] }
[577](https://docs.rs#577)            }
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        }
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    }
[580](https://docs.rs#580)}

# all_tuples in variadics_please - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/variadics_please/2.0.0/variadics_please/macro.all_tuples.html

`all_tuples!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids. Useful to generate scaffolding to work around Rust
lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`
invokes `impl_foo` providing ident tuples through arity `start..end`.
If you require the length of the tuple, see [ all_tuples_with_size!](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples_with_size.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#single-parameter)Single parameter

```
struct Foo<T> {
    // ..
}
trait WrappedInFoo {
    type Tup;
}
macro_rules! impl_wrapped_in_foo {
    ($($T:ident),*) => {
        impl<$($T),*> WrappedInFoo for ($($T,)*) {
            type Tup = ($(Foo<$T>,)*);
        }
    };
}
// start from 0 element to 15 elements
all_tuples!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 0, 15, T);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!();
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0, T1);
// ..
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(T0 .. T14);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multiple-parameters)Multiple parameters

```
trait Append {
    type Out<Item>;
    fn append<Item>(tup: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item>;
}
impl Append for () {
    type Out<Item> = (Item,);
    fn append<Item>(_: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
        (item,)
    }
}
macro_rules! impl_append {
    ($(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
        impl<$($P),*> Append for ($($P,)*) {
            type Out<Item> = ($($P),*, Item);
            fn append<Item>(($($p,)*): Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
                ($($p),*, item)
            }
        }
    }
}
// start from 1 element to 15 elements
all_tuples!(impl_append, 1, 15, P, p);
// impl_append!((P0, p0));
// impl_append!((P0, p0), (P1, p1));
// impl_append!((P0, p0), (P1, p1), (P2, p2));
// ..
// impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P14, p14));
// start from 16 elements to 20
all_tuples!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
// impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P15, p15));
// ..
// impl_append!((P0, p0) .. (P19, p19));
```
`#[doc(fake_variadic)]`

To improve the readability of your docs when implementing a trait for
tuples or fn pointers of varying length you can use the rustdoc-internal `fake_variadic` marker.
All your impls are collapsed and shown as a single `impl Trait for (F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ)`.

The `all_tuples!` macro does most of the work for you, the only change to your implementation macro
is that you have to accept attributes using `$(#[$meta:meta])*`.

Since this feature requires a nightly compiler, it’s only enabled on docs.rs by default. Add the following to your lib.rs if not already present:

```
// `rustdoc_internals` is needed for `#[doc(fake_variadics)]`
#![cfg_attr(any(docsrs, docsrs_dep), feature(rustdoc_internals))]
```
```
trait Variadic {}
impl Variadic for () {}
macro_rules! impl_variadic {
    ($(#[$meta:meta])* $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
        $(#[$meta])*
        impl<$($P),*> Variadic for ($($P,)*) {}
    }
}
all_tuples!(#[doc(fake_variadic)] impl_variadic, 1, 15, P, p);
```

# all_tuples_with_size in variadics_please - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/variadics_please/2.0.0/variadics_please/macro.all_tuples_with_size.html

`all_tuples_with_size!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids with their length. Useful to generate scaffolding to
work around Rust lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples_with_size!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`
invokes `impl_foo` providing ident tuples through arity `start..end` preceded by their length.
If you don’t require the length of the tuple, see [ all_tuples!](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#single-parameter)Single parameter

```
struct Foo<T> {
    // ..
}
trait WrappedInFoo {
    type Tup;
    const LENGTH: usize;
}
macro_rules! impl_wrapped_in_foo {
    ($N:expr, $($T:ident),*) => {
        impl<$($T),*> WrappedInFoo for ($($T,)*) {
            type Tup = ($(Foo<$T>,)*);
            const LENGTH: usize = $N;
        }
    };
}
all_tuples_with_size!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 0, 15, T);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(0);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(1, T0);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(2, T0, T1);
// ..
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(15, T0 .. T14);
all_tuples_with_size!(impl_wrapped_in_foo, 16, 20, T);
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(16, T0 .. T15);
// ..
// impl_wrapped_in_foo!(20, T0 .. T19);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multiple-parameters)Multiple parameters

```
trait Append {
    type Out<Item>;
    fn append<Item>(tup: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item>;
}
impl Append for () {
    type Out<Item> = (Item,);
    fn append<Item>(_: Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
        (item,)
    }
}
macro_rules! impl_append {
    ($N:expr, $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
        impl<$($P),*> Append for ($($P,)*) {
            type Out<Item> = ($($P),*, Item);
            fn append<Item>(($($p,)*): Self, item: Item) -> Self::Out<Item> {
                ($($p),*, item)
            }
        }
    }
}
all_tuples_with_size!(impl_append, 1, 15, P, p);
// impl_append!(1, (P0, p0));
// impl_append!(2, (P0, p0), (P1, p1));
// impl_append!(3, (P0, p0), (P1, p1), (P2, p2));
// ..
// impl_append!(15, (P0, p0) .. (P14, p14));
all_tuples_with_size!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
// impl_append!(16, (P0, p0) .. (P15, p15));
// ..
// impl_append!(20, (P0, p0) .. (P19, p19));
```
`#[doc(fake_variadic)]`

To improve the readability of your docs when implementing a trait for
tuples or fn pointers of varying length you can use the rustdoc-internal `fake_variadic` marker.
All your impls are collapsed and shown as a single `impl Trait for (F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ)`.

The `all_tuples!` macro does most of the work for you, the only change to your implementation macro
is that you have to accept attributes using `$(#[$meta:meta])*`.

Since this feature requires a nightly compiler, it’s only enabled on docs.rs by default. Add the following to your lib.rs if not already present:

```
// `rustdoc_internals` is needed for `#[doc(fake_variadics)]`
#![cfg_attr(any(docsrs, docsrs_dep), feature(rustdoc_internals))]
```
```
trait Variadic {}
impl Variadic for () {}
macro_rules! impl_variadic {
    ($N:expr, $(#[$meta:meta])* $(($P:ident, $p:ident)),*) => {
        $(#[$meta])*
        impl<$($P),*> Variadic for ($($P,)*) {}
    }
}
all_tuples_with_size!(#[doc(fake_variadic)] impl_variadic, 1, 15, P, p);
```

# all_tuples_enumerated in variadics_please - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/variadics_please/2.0.0/variadics_please/macro.all_tuples_enumerated.html

`all_tuples_enumerated!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

A variant of [ all_tuples!](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples.html) that enumerates its output.

In particular, the tuples used by the inner macro will themselves be composed of tuples which contain the index.

For example, with a single parameter:

```
trait Squawk {
    fn squawk(&self);
}
// If every type in a tuple is `Squawk`, the tuple can squawk by having its
// constituents squawk sequentially:
macro_rules! impl_squawk {
    ($(($n:tt, $T:ident)),*) => {
        impl<$($T: Squawk),*> Squawk for ($($T,)*) {
            fn squawk(&self) {
                $(
                    self.$n.squawk();
                )*
            }
        }
    };
}
all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 1, 15, T);
// impl_squawk!((0, T0));
// impl_squawk!((0, T0), (1, T1));
// ..
// impl_squawk!((0, T0) .. (14, T14));
all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 16, 20, T);
// impl_append!((0, T0) .. (15, T15));
// ..
// impl_append!((0, T0) .. (19, T19));
```
With multiple parameters, the result is similar, but with the additional parameters included in each tuple; e.g.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_squawk, 1, 15, P, p);
// impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0));
// impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0), (1, P1, p1));
// ..
// impl_squawk!((0, P0, p0) .. (14, P14, p14));
all_tuples_enumerated!(impl_append, 16, 20, P, p);
// impl_append!((0, P0, p0) .. (15, P15, p15));
// ..
// impl_append!((0, P0, p0) .. (19, P19, p19));
```

# variadics_please - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/variadics_please/latest/variadics_please/

## Expand description

Provides macros for implementing traits on variadic types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [all_](https://docs.rs/macro.all_tuples.html)- tuples
- Helper macro to generate tuple pyramids. Useful to generate scaffolding to work around Rust
lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`. If you require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples_with_size!`

work around Rust lacking variadics. Invoking `all_tuples_with_size!(impl_foo, start, end, P, Q, ..)`invokes`impl_foo`providing ident tuples through arity`start..end`preceded by their length. If you don’t require the length of the tuple, see`all_tuples!`

# quote 1.0.46 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/quote/^1.0

# Rust Quasi-Quoting

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller's crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text editor
or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor's brace matching, syntax
highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than compiling
that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass it around,
mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens to compile into
the macro caller's crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Syntax

The quote crate provides a [ quote!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote.html) macro within which you can write Rust code
that gets packaged into a

[and can be treated as data. You should think of](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html)

`TokenStream``TokenStream` as representing a fragment of Rust source code.Within the `quote!` macro, interpolation is done with `#var`. Any type
implementing the [ quote::ToTokens](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/trait.ToTokens.html) trait can be interpolated. This includes
most Rust primitive types as well as most of the syntax tree types from

[.](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)

`syn````
let tokens = quote! ;
```
## Repetition

Repetition is done using `#(...)*` or `#(...),*` similar to `macro_rules!`. This
iterates through the elements of any variable interpolated within the repetition
and inserts a copy of the repetition body for each one. The variables in an
interpolation may be a `Vec`, slice, `BTreeSet`, or any `Iterator`.

- `#(#var)*`— no separators
- `#(#var),*`— the character before the asterisk is used as a separator
- `#( struct #var; )*`— the repetition can contain other things
- `#( #k => println!("{}", #v), )*`— even multiple interpolations

Note that there is a difference between `#(#var ,)*` and `#(#var),*`—the latter
does not produce a trailing comma. This matches the behavior of delimiters in
`macro_rules!`.

## Returning tokens to the compiler

The `quote!` macro evaluates to an expression of type
`proc_macro2::TokenStream`. Meanwhile Rust procedural macros are expected to
return the type `proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The difference between the two types is that `proc_macro` types are entirely
specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a
procedural macro, while `proc_macro2` types may exist anywhere including tests
and non-macro code like main.rs and build.rs. This is why even the procedural
macro ecosystem is largely built around `proc_macro2`, because that ensures the
libraries are unit testable and accessible in non-macro contexts.

There is a [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.From.html)-conversion in both directions so returning the output of

`quote!` from a procedural macro usually looks like `tokens.into()` or
`proc_macro::TokenStream::from(tokens)`.## Examples

### Combining quoted fragments

Usually you don't end up constructing an entire final `TokenStream` in one
piece. Different parts may come from different helper functions. The tokens
produced by `quote!` themselves implement `ToTokens` and so can be interpolated
into later `quote!` invocations to build up a final result.

```
let type_definition = quote! ;
let methods = quote! ;
let tokens = quote! ;
```
### Constructing identifiers

Suppose we have an identifier `ident` which came from somewhere in a macro
input and we need to modify it in some way for the macro output. Let's consider
prepending the identifier with an underscore.

Simply interpolating the identifier next to an underscore will not have the
behavior of concatenating them. The underscore and the identifier will continue
to be two separate tokens as if you had written `_ x`.

```
// incorrect
quote!
```
The solution is to build a new identifier token with the correct value. As this
is such a common case, the `format_ident!` macro provides a convenient utility
for doing so correctly.

```
let varname = format_ident!;
quote!
```
Alternatively, the APIs provided by Syn and proc-macro2 can be used to directly
build the identifier. This is roughly equivalent to the above, but will not
handle `ident` being a raw identifier.

```
let concatenated = format!;
let varname = new;
quote!
```
### Making method calls

Let's say our macro requires some type specified in the macro input to have a
constructor called `new`. We have the type in a variable called `field_type` of
type `syn::Type` and want to invoke the constructor.

```
// incorrect
quote!
```
This works only sometimes. If `field_type` is `String`, the expanded code
contains `String::new()` which is fine. But if `field_type` is something like
`Vec<i32>` then the expanded code is `Vec<i32>::new()` which is invalid syntax.
Ordinarily in handwritten Rust we would write `Vec::<i32>::new()` but for macros
often the following is more convenient.

```
quote!
```
This expands to `<Vec<i32>>::new()` which behaves correctly.

A similar pattern is appropriate for trait methods.

```
quote!
```
## Hygiene

Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
`ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within a `quote!` invocation
are spanned with [ Span::call_site()](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html#method.call_site).

A different span can be provided explicitly through the [ quote_spanned!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote_spanned.html)
macro.

## Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through [prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease)
before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated code it is
convenient for a human to read and debug.

Be aware that no kind of hygiene or span information is retained when tokens are written to a file; the conversion from tokens to source code is lossy.

Example usage in build.rs:

```
let output = quote! ;
let syntax_tree = parse2.unwrap;
let formatted = unparse;
let out_dir = var_os.unwrap;
let dest_path = new.join;
write.unwrap;
```

# unsynn 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unsynn/^0.3

unsynn (from german 'unsinn' for nonsense) is a minimalist rust parser library. It achieves this by leaving out the actual grammar implementations which are implemented in distinct crates. Still it comes with batteries included, there are parsers, combinators and transformers to solve most parsing tasks.

In exchange it offers simple composeable Parsers and declarative Parser construction. Grammars will be implemented in their own crates (see unsynn-rust).

It is primarily intended use is when one wants to create proc macros for rust that define their own grammar or need only sparse rust parsers.

Other uses can be building parsers for gramars outside a rust/proc-macro context. Unsynn can
parse any `&str` data (The tokenizer step relies on `proc_macro2`).

# Examples

## Creating and Parsing Custom Types

The [ unsynn!{}](crate::unsynn!) macro generates the [

`Parser`] and [`ToTokens`] implementations for your types.Notice that unsynn implements [`Parser`] and [`ToTokens`] for many standard rust types. Like
we use `u32` in this example.

```
# use *;
let mut token_iter = "foo ( 1, 2, 3 )".to_token_iter;
unsynn!
// iter.parse() is from the IParse trait
let ast: IdentThenParenthesisedNumbers = token_iter.parse.unwrap;
assert_tokens_eq!;
```
In case the automatiically generated [`Parser`] and [`ToTokens`] implementations are not
sufficient the macro supports custom parsing and token emission through [ parse_with](crate::unsynn#custom-parsing-with-parse_with) and

[clauses:](crate::unsynn#custom-token-emission-with-to_tokens)

`to_tokens`- `from Type:`- `parse_with`
- `parse_with`- `from`for transformation)
- `to_tokens`

The [ parse_with](crate::unsynn#custom-parsing-with-parse_with) and

[clauses are independent and optional. The](crate::unsynn#custom-token-emission-with-to_tokens)

`to_tokens`[clause must be used together with](crate::unsynn#custom-parsing-with-parse_with)

`from`[. When more control is needed, the implementations can also be written manually.](crate::unsynn#custom-parsing-with-parse_with)

`parse_with`### Custom Parsing and `ToTokens`

Example of custom parsing and token emission - parse emoji as bools, emit as emoji:

```

```
See the [COOKBOOK](https://docs.rs/crate#cookbook) for more details on [ parse_with](crate::unsynn#custom-parsing-with-parse_with)
and

`to_tokens`## Using Composition

Composition can be used without defining new datatypes. This is useful for simple parsers or
when one wants to parse things on the fly which are desconstructed immediately. See the
[ combinator](crate::combinator) module for more composition types.

```
# use *;
// We parse this below
let mut token_iter = "foo ( 1, 2, 3 )".to_token_iter;
// Type::parse() is from the Parse trait
let ast =

        parse.unwrap;
assert_tokens_eq!;
```
## Custom Operators and Keywords

Keywords and operators can be defined within the [ unsynn!{}](crate::unsynn!) macro:

```
# use *;
unsynn!
// Build expression parser with proper precedence
type Expression = ;
type AdditiveExpr = ;
